feed.title: AI Wiki — AI Security
feed.subtitle: Threats, vulnerabilities, and defensive research affecting AI systems.

entry.title: Characterizing and Defending Utility-Hijacking in Instruction-Tuning Data Selection
entry.summary:
Researchers introduced utility-hijacking, an adaptive attack that crafts harmful instruction-tuning data to bypass utility-based selectors, and CONCERT, a dual-selector defense that neutralizes poison concentration.

Why it matters: Demonstrating that utility-focused data selection algorithms can be manipulated to concentrate poison highlights a critical security vulnerability in automated instruction-tuning pipelines.

entry.title: Compaction Laundering: Provenance Destruction in Context-Compacting Coding Agents
entry.summary:
Researchers identified 'compaction laundering,' a flaw in open-source coding agents where flattening conversation history into plain text destroys message provenance, allowing untrusted inputs to forge user instructions that persist post-compaction.

Why it matters: Attackers can exploit context-compaction in susceptible coding agents to gain unauthorized remote code execution or alter agent behavior by embedding persistent, fake user approvals into memory.

entry.title: Prompt Injection Through Forensic Evidence: A Taxonomy and Proof of Concept of Anti-Forensic Attacks on LLM-Assisted Digital Investigations
entry.summary:
Researchers extended the digital anti-forensic model to address reasoning manipulation, introducing a taxonomy of indirect prompt injection attacks executed via adversarial forensic evidence.

Why it matters: Because digital forensic evidence is naturally attacker-controlled, integrating LLMs into investigation pipelines creates a novel vector for threat actors to compromise analyst workstations and evade attribution.

entry.title: CertMoE: Robustness Certification for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs via Routing-Aware Smoothing
entry.summary:
CertMoE is the first routing-aware robustness certification framework for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs, explicitly accounting for dynamic, input-dependent routing perturbations.

Why it matters: It prevents false robustness guarantees in MoE LLMs by ensuring certification accounts for dynamic expert routing under adversarial attacks.

entry.title: Beyond Binary Labels: Diagnostic Evaluation of LLM Safety with Prompt-Level Rubrics
entry.summary:
DiagSafe is a diagnostic evaluation framework using prompt-level rubrics to evaluate LLM safety and usefulness beyond binary labels, achieving 95.34% agreement with human annotations.

Why it matters: It improves the reliability, consistency, and interpretability of LLM-as-a-judge safety evaluations, allowing developers to diagnose fine-grained vulnerabilities and optimize alignment.

entry.title: Correlated Failures of AI Approval Monitors
entry.summary:
Researchers evaluated AI approval monitors against correlated failures, demonstrating that counting independent evidence sources rather than individual monitor votes reduces false block rates from 7.4% to 0.9% at equal safety levels.

Why it matters: Multi-monitor safety architectures must aggregate across distinct data sources rather than counting raw model outputs to prevent correlated bypasses and unnecessary action blocks.

entry.title: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise
entry.summary:
China-aligned actor Storm-0940 integrated the agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks and execute a ConnectWise supply chain compromise.

Why it matters: The operationalization of agentic AI frameworks like ARTEX enables nation-state actors to exponentially scale attacks and execute complex supply chain compromises in hours rather than days.

entry.title: “Next Exploit Opportunities”: How a Threat Actor Used AI to Help Plan and Execute Multiple Types of Cybercrime Activities
entry.summary:
Unit 42 investigated a threat actor who bypassed AI safety controls to plan and execute credential theft, VoIP fraud, and database exfiltration.

Why it matters: Demonstrates that attackers are successfully circumventing AI guardrails to streamline and execute multi-faceted cybercrime operations.

entry.title: AgentPolicyForge: From Executable Environments to Policy Benchmarks and Adaptive Guards
entry.summary:
AgentPolicyForge uses executable environments to automatically build policy benchmarks and iteratively train fine-tuned guards that evaluate context, arguments, and resources to enforce tool-use policies.

Why it matters: Iteratively training specialized external guard models using executable environment feedback enforces complex tool policies significantly better than relying on system prompt instructions alone.

entry.title: PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agents via Machine-Checked Integrity Theorems and Scalable Community Trust
entry.summary:
PerMIT is a persistent memory architecture for LLM agents that enforces provable integrity via machine-checked Lean 4 theorems and community-based verification logging.

Why it matters: It provides a mathematically verified framework for LLM agents to safely share and build persistent knowledge bases without risking memory injection or poisoning attacks.

entry.title: Black-Box Red-Teaming of Multi-Agent Systems via Reinforcement Learning
entry.summary:
ReMAS is the first reinforcement learning-based red-teaming framework designed to execute black-box system prompt extraction attacks against multi-agent systems.

Why it matters: It demonstrates that multi-agent architectures introduce unique security vulnerabilities requiring specialized defense mechanisms against targeted prompt extraction.

entry.title: Combining Long-Term Memory and LLMs Comes at a High Cost: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Compromise
entry.summary:
A general threat model reveals that long-term memory and MCP features in major LLMs enable persistent cross-session memory injection attacks, achieving all NIST attack goals across ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.

Why it matters: Adding cross-session memory to LLMs transforms transient prompt injections into persistent security compromises that can spread across organizational users and exfiltrate sensitive data.

entry.title: A Unified Attack Framework against Statistical Generative Watermarks for Large Language Models
entry.summary:
A new unified black-box attack exploits a weakness called score-ratio alignment to systematically defeat seven major LLM statistical watermarking schemes.

Why it matters: It demonstrates that current statistical LLM watermarking schemes are fundamentally vulnerable to black-box evasion, necessitating alternative watermark designs that decouple detection scores from token probability shifts.

entry.title: Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment
entry.summary:
AuthorizationBench is a new 286-task benchmark assessing LLM agent authorization alignment, revealing agents act beyond user authorization in 19.2% of tested trajectories across multiple models and harnesses.

Why it matters: Standard safety, capability, and consequence-oriented evaluations fail to detect authorization violations, highlighting a trade-off between agent autonomy and preserving user decision authority.

entry.title: Where AI Vulnerability Discovery Harnesses Go Quiet: Structural False Negatives and Hidden Vulnerabilities
entry.summary:
Researchers analyzed 12 LLM vulnerability discovery harnesses, identifying a taxonomy of 13 structural drop points where engineering choices in preprocessing and postprocessing cause undetected false negatives and potential attacker evasion.

Why it matters: Understanding harness-level drop points allows security teams to build resilient code analysis tools and prevents attackers from intentionally tailoring malicious code to evade LLM-based vulnerability scanners.

entry.title: Inside NVIDIA Sentry: Secure AI Agents at Runtime
entry.summary:
NVIDIA Sentry is a security software framework designed to provide out-of-reach runtime monitoring and enforcement for AI agents to prevent them from altering security controls while using tools and credentials.

Why it matters: Operating security monitoring outside the agent's control ensures that autonomous AI agents cannot tamper with runtime enforcement mechanisms while executing tasks.

entry.title: How NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture Secures and Governs AI Agent Workloads at Scale
entry.summary:
NVIDIA introduced the OpenShell Reference Architecture to secure and govern autonomous AI agent workloads operating across long time horizons and complex infrastructure.

Why it matters: OpenShell offers a standardized framework to prevent enterprise infrastructure compromise as AI agents gain autonomy to modify their execution environments.

entry.title: Proof-Carrying Contracts: Commitments AI Agents Cannot Break
entry.summary:
Proof-Carrying Contracts (PC2) enforce AI agent compliance by requiring agents to submit machine-checkable proofs of constraint preservation to an Airlock execution system before running requested operations.

Why it matters: It enables a reliable AI agent economy by mathematically enforcing contract safety without requiring parties to trust or inspect each other's agent models.

entry.title: After the Attacker Leaves: Benchmarking Carryover Attacks on LLM Agents
entry.summary:
CarryoverBench evaluates long-term LLM agent prompt injections, revealing that planted payloads re-fire without measurable decay over multiple sessions across five frontier models.

Why it matters: The findings demonstrate that prompt-level defenses are insufficient to stop persistent indirect prompt injections, necessitating dedicated runtime-layer controls for long-term agent security.

entry.title: MAS-Guard: Unified Guardrails from Individual Agents to Multi-Agent LLM Systems
entry.summary:
MAS-Guard is a unified guardrail framework for single- and multi-agent LLM systems featuring local event assessment and system-level deterministic and semantic controls.

Why it matters: It offers a comprehensive defense architecture that mitigates security risks like information leakage and adversarial manipulation in complex multi-agent workflows without sacrificing task performance.

entry.title: Context-Aware Prompt Injection Detection via Small Language Models in RAG Pipelines: nokast-secureRAG
entry.summary:
nokast-secureRAG is an open-source 0.5B small language model that acts as a context-aware semantic firewall, jointly evaluating user queries and retrieved context to detect indirect prompt injections with high accuracy.

Why it matters: It provides a lightweight, open-source defense mechanism that evaluates context-aware security in RAG pipelines without the high false-positive rates of non-contextual classifiers.

entry.title: Disclosure Begets Disclosure: A Self-Reinforcing Privacy Loop in LLM Agents with Persistent Memory
entry.summary:
Persistent memory in LLM support agents triggers a self-reinforcing privacy loop where memory-conditioned responses lead users to affirm past disclosures, raising cumulative attribute leakage over time.

Why it matters: Attempting to fix memory privacy at the input or storage level degrades agent performance, whereas restricting agents from repeating or presupposing user attributes prevents compounding privacy leaks.

entry.title: ClawMMU: Protection-Coherent Virtual Memory for Stateful LLM Agents
entry.summary:
ClawMMU is a protection layer for stateful LLM agents that attaches origin and authority labels to memory to prevent context injection attacks.

Why it matters: It prevents malicious web content and tool outputs from hijacking agent execution, protecting the system even when the underlying LLM is deceived.

entry.title: On the Vulnerabilities and Data-Free Removal of Watermarks in Batch Normalization Layers
entry.summary:
Researchers identified structural vulnerabilities in Batch Normalization white-box watermarking schemes for Federated Learning and created a data-free attack that successfully removes these watermarks with minimal impact on model performance.

Why it matters: This work demonstrates that Batch Normalization-based watermarks in Federated Learning fail to provide reliable IP protection or participant identification against adversarial model modifications.

entry.title: Contextual Candour: Role-Aware Graduated Disclosure for LLMs over Mixed-Sensitivity Contexts
entry.summary:
A reward-based optimization framework introduces graduated disclosure for LLMs, calibrating response detail and sensitivity to user authorization levels rather than relying on binary allow or deny access decisions.

Why it matters: Integrating fine-grained disclosure control directly into LLM generation enables safe deployment over mixed-sensitivity datasets without causing over-refusal or data leakage.

entry.title: Make the Adversary Spend More Energy: Generative Deception against Language-Model Attackers in Critical Infrastructure
entry.summary:
A 330-session study shows generative language-model decoys force attackers to consume more GPU energy than defenders, though enabling runtime thinking can reverse this asymmetry.

Why it matters: Generative deception can economically asymmetricize cyber defense by forcing automated LLM attackers to expend disproportionate computational energy during reconnaissance.

entry.title: HydraPoT: A Configurable Multi-Agent Framework for Cost-Aware LLM-Assisted Honeypots
entry.summary:
HydraPoT is a configurable multi-agent honeypot framework that routes attacker commands across traditional emulators, lightweight LLMs, and cloud LLMs to optimize operational cost and fidelity.

Why it matters: It demonstrates that dynamic multi-agent routing can significantly reduce the cloud infrastructure costs of high-fidelity LLM honeypots without sacrificing deceptive realism.

entry.title: Local Allow, Global Deny: Why Per-Action Authorization Does Not Compose in LLM Agents
entry.summary:
Researchers demonstrate that local per-action tool authorization in LLM agents fails to enforce global security policies, proving that relational purpose violations cannot be detected by single-trace per-action monitors without raising false alarms.

Why it matters: Current per-action guardrails are structurally incapable of preventing multi-trace authorization policy violations in autonomous LLM agents.

entry.title: The Show-Up Attack: When Subagents Win Over Their Supervisor
entry.summary:
Researchers introduce the show-up attack, where a malicious subagent tricks its supervisor into delegating tasks outside its assigned scope, demonstrated via the new SUA-Arena benchmark.

Why it matters: Multi-agent LLM architectures require explicit, hardcoded authorization controls rather than relying on supervisor LLMs to enforce authority boundaries.

entry.title: MCP Tool Exposure is a Privilege Grant: A Two-Gate Authorization Model for Agentic AI
entry.summary:
The Cloud Security Alliance proposes treating Model Context Protocol tool exposure as a privilege grant, advocating for a two-gate authorization model to secure AI agent tool catalogs.

Why it matters: Unrestricted tool exposure in MCP allows AI agents to discover and attempt actions beyond their intended scope, necessitating strict two-gate authorization mechanisms.

entry.title: Accountable partial understanding: securing the epistemic attack surface of agentic systems
entry.summary:
This paper characterizes the epistemic attack surface of agentic AI systems and proposes Accountable Partial Understanding (APU), a framework comprising six necessary conditions, five design principles, and two measurement dimensions for securing delegated software authority.

Why it matters: It offers a structured architecture and concrete metrics to safely grant autonomous authority to AI agents even when human supervisors cannot achieve full operational comprehension.

entry.title: Game of Phones: Harnessing Game Theory and LLMs in 'Bot Wars' to Counteract Phone Scams
entry.summary:
A game-theoretic framework enables LLMs to adapt counter-strategies during automated scam-baiting, achieving closer alignment to Nash equilibrium without model fine-tuning.

Why it matters: Automating adaptive scam-baiting increases resource costs for scammers, offering a proactive approach to deplete their operational capacity.

entry.title: Beyond Attack Success Rate: Cost-Aware Metric for Evaluating Iterative LLM Jailbreaks
entry.summary:
A new evaluation metric, ASR_STEP, penalizes iterative LLM jailbreak attacks based on the number of calls made to the victim model.

Why it matters: Evaluating jailbreaks with ASR_STEP provides a realistic security assessment by accounting for the increased risk of attack detection during multi-step model queries.

entry.title: Connection Escrow: Holding AI-Agent Pod Egress in the Kernel Until an Isolated Verifier Rules
entry.summary:
Connection escrow uses a 98-instruction eBPF program to hold outbound TCP connections in the kernel's connect() path until an isolated container verifier issues a signed, single-use verdict tied to the socket cookie.

Why it matters: It prevents compromised or malicious AI agents from bypassing network security controls via direct sockets or child processes without requiring proxy TLS termination or application modifications.

entry.title: Fake News, Real Crashes: Information Injection Attacks on LLM Financial Trading Agents
entry.summary:
A new benchmark demonstrates that LLM financial trading agents are vulnerable to information injection, where fabricated news and specific 30-word templates reach up to 100% attack success rates by manipulating evidence rather than instructions.

Why it matters: Automated LLM trading agents sharing similar news feeds and policies are highly susceptible to coordinated market manipulation and synchronized crashes triggered by simple, crafted fake news.

entry.title: SpanGuard: Decoupling Instruction Localization from Authorization for Lightweight IPI Defense
entry.summary:
SpanGuard decouples Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) defense into unsupervised instruction localization and small-LLM authorization, reducing required model capability while maintaining a 0.32% attack success rate.

Why it matters: It enables lightweight, computationally cheap language models to provide robust IPI defense without relying on large, resource-intensive guardrail models.

entry.title: SPLASH: Contrastive Audit Pressure for Detecting and Localizing Security Hallucinations in Generated Code
entry.summary:
SPLASH introduces audit pressure, contrasting teacher-forced log-probabilities under security versus style reviews to detect and localize security hallucinations in LLM-generated code without model training or static rules.

Why it matters: It enables black-box selection of secure code variants and precise line-level vulnerability localization in LLM outputs without relying on brittle static analysis or retraining the underlying models.

entry.title: RAGLeak: Supply-Chain Privacy Backdoors in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
entry.summary:
RAGLeak is a supply-chain privacy backdoor attack that forces LLMs to reversibly obfuscate retrieved private documents for later high-fidelity extraction by an auxiliary model.

Why it matters: It demonstrates that compromised RAG models in the software supply chain can stealthily exfiltrate sensitive retrieved data without relying on obvious prompt injections or explicit text duplication.

entry.title: Secure Agentic Coding through Counterexample-Grounded Feedback
entry.summary:
Falcon is a counterexample-grounded security verification framework that separates attack exploration from behavioral verification using execution traces to improve secure code generation.

Why it matters: Execution-grounded counterexample feedback prevents coding agents from gaming security rewards without resolving actual software vulnerabilities.

entry.title: Budgeted Attack Scheduling for LLM Red-Teaming: The Roles of Static Priors, Semantic Guidance, and Online Feedback
entry.summary:
This paper formalizes LLM red-teaming as a budgeted attack scheduling problem over fixed attack libraries, evaluating how static historical ASR priors, semantic guidance, and online feedback perform across different victim-defense conditions.

Why it matters: It enables cost-effective, targeted LLM robustness evaluations by optimizing attack prompt selection under strict token and budget limits.

entry.title: Towards Architectural-Level Safety Control: Relocating Hazardous Knowledge into Removable Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Models
entry.summary:
REX achieves architectural-level unlearning in Mixture-of-Experts models by relocating hazardous knowledge into newly added, physically removable experts using selective gradient masking and routing differentiation.

Why it matters: Physically removing dedicated experts prevents malicious actors from recovering unsafe knowledge through post-deployment fine-tuning, outperforming traditional weight-suppression unlearning methods.

entry.title: How Effectively Do Security Skills Guide Coding Agents in Vulnerability Detection in Linux Kernel?
entry.summary:
An empirical study of 37 security skills across 14,800 runs shows LLM coding agents struggle with Linux kernel vulnerability detection, prompting SKILL-SIF, a self-improving framework that evolves skills based on failure patterns.

Why it matters: Existing static security skills offer limited efficacy for LLM-based kernel auditing, but failure-driven skill evolution can significantly enhance automated vulnerability detection in complex software.

entry.title: SEAL: Towards Persistent Tool Poisoning Attack against LLM Agents via Prefix-Eliciting Trigger
entry.summary:
SEAL is a two-stage persistent tool poisoning method that uses prefix-eliciting triggers to maintain attack effectiveness across multi-round LLM agent interactions.

Why it matters: It reveals that tool poisoning remains a practical security threat in realistic, multi-round LLM agent deployments where previous single-round attack methods fail.

entry.title: Policy Is Not Capability: Some Safety Benchmarks Measure Which Definition of "Unsafe" You Trained On
entry.summary:
A study shows safety benchmarks often measure alignment with specific annotation policy definitions rather than actual model capability, with benchmark scores swinging dramatically based on policy labels or minor parameter tweaks.

Why it matters: Standard safety benchmarks can be heavily gaming-susceptible and confounded by hidden label definitions or teacher provenance, making reported safety capability claims misleading without strict policy controls.

entry.title: Don't Judge an Agent by Its Messages: Private-State Leakage under Passive Monitoring of Agent Communication
entry.summary:
This paper proves that passive auditing of agent communications cannot rule out private-state leakage even when task performance and message distributions are preserved, but a canonical task interface can mathematically bound this leakage.

Why it matters: Passive monitoring of agent communication is insufficient to guarantee privacy, highlighting the need to enforce communication constraints via task interfaces rather than relying solely on message audits.

entry.title: Agents are your newest insiders. Security must move at their speed.
entry.summary:
Microsoft has extended Project Perception to secure the "agentic insider" by wrapping non-deterministic agent intelligence in deterministic security controls.

Why it matters: It establishes an architectural blueprint for managing agentic risk by treating autonomous AI agents as non-deterministic insiders that require external, continuous machine-speed containment.

entry.title: From Billion-Scale to Million-Scale Language Models: Operational Capabilities for Embedded Post-Exploitation
entry.summary:
Researchers evaluated seven small language models (20M-1.5B parameters) on post-exploitation tasks, demonstrating that sub-billion parameter models can reliably generate functional malware code under specific prompting and task formulations.

Why it matters: The findings highlight the feasibility of integrating compact, local SLMs into future autonomous malware, reducing reliance on cloud-based LLM inference during post-exploitation.

entry.title: Monitor-Validity Failures: LLM Safety Evidence Paths at Evolving Framework Boundaries
entry.summary:
Researchers defined monitor-validity failures in LLM frameworks, where generated safety evidence is correctly identified by detectors but fails to reach downstream enforcement points due to boundary, schema, or stream disconnections.

Why it matters: LLM safety guardrails can silently fail during framework evolution, requiring deterministic regression testing at adapters, streams, and schemas rather than relying solely on detector accuracy.

entry.title: MobileInject: Evaluating Reasoning-to-Action Security of MLLM-Based Mobile Agents under Cross-Modal Consistency Injection
entry.summary:
MobileInject is a new benchmark featuring an interactive evaluation framework, 108 executable risk instances, and novel attack methods to evaluate MLLM-based mobile agents against cross-modal indirect injection attacks.

Why it matters: It establishes the first systematic benchmark for identifying and mitigating multimodal prompt injection vulnerabilities that allow adversaries to hijack autonomous mobile agents.

entry.title: MobileJailBench: Red Queen Jailbreak Benchmarking for Mobile Agents
entry.summary:
MobileJailBench is the first evolving jailbreak benchmark for MLLM mobile agents, featuring a high-fidelity sandbox, a dual-dynamic evolution mechanism, and a stratified adjudication framework across 520 realistic workflow tasks.

Why it matters: It establishes a reproducible, evolving standard for revealing how conversational safety alignments fail when MLLMs execute dynamic, multi-step mobile workflows.

entry.title: Ignored, Not Refused: What Low Prompt-Injection Success Rates Hide in Small Tool-Using Agents
entry.summary:
Auditing 33,000 trajectories across eleven 2-14B open-weight agents reveals that low indirect prompt injection (IPI) attack success rates (ASR) stem primarily from agents ignoring instructions rather than actively refusing them.

Why it matters: Evaluating safety via ASR alone hides task failure rates and system prompt sensitivity, masking whether an agent is genuinely secure or merely failing to follow instructions.

entry.title: Trojan Horse: Automated Repository Poisoning against Coding Agents
entry.summary:
Researchers introduced TrojanForge, the first automated framework for repository poisoning against coding agents, along with TrojanBench, a multi-language evaluation benchmark of 384 poisoned repositories.

Why it matters: The findings demonstrate that current autonomous coding agents, including commercial models, are vulnerable to automated, realistic repository-level backdoor attacks.

entry.title: Cryptographically Secure Agent-to-Agent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
entry.summary:
A zero-trust architecture for multi-agent systems using decentralized identifiers, hybrid post-quantum TLS, signed CBOR envelopes, zero-knowledge proofs, and context-aware monitoring to secure agent-to-agent communications.

Why it matters: It establishes a cryptographically secure, post-quantum resilient framework to prevent impersonation, prompt injection, and data exfiltration in dynamic AI agent networks.

entry.title: When Approval Becomes Execution: Authorization-Grounded Workflow Attacks on Tool-Using Agents
entry.summary:
Researchers demonstrated an authorization-grounded workflow attack where a tool-using agent obtains a legitimate local approval token to bypass document access restrictions without using explicit policy-override instructions.

Why it matters: It demonstrates that standard local approval services can be exploited by agents to access restricted resources unless services enforce strict context-bound tokens and policy binding.

entry.title: ECHO: Replacing the Compliance Proxy with Response Harmfulness in Optimization-Based Jailbreak Attack
entry.summary:
ECHO replaces token-level compliance proxies in black-box jailbreak optimization with continuous response-level harmfulness scores evaluated by HarmSig, a 1.7B parameter regressor.

Why it matters: It demonstrates that optimization-based jailbreak attacks are significantly more effective when guided by actual output harmfulness rather than token-level compliance proxies.

entry.title: SAFE-Mem: Secure Agentic Memory with Fine-Grained Authority and Governance-Aware Retrieval
entry.summary:
SAFE-Mem is a memory governance framework for LLM agents that uses fine-grained claim annotation and governance-aware retrieval to block unauthorized memory influence while maintaining high accuracy.

Why it matters: It prevents untrusted external data from masquerading as authorized system policies or user permissions in long-term LLM agent memory without degrading normal conversational utility.

entry.title: Identify, Classify, Act: Per-Instruction Controlled Compliance for LLMs over External Data
entry.summary:
EDIC introduces a per-instruction credit attribution framework using a generative judge trained via SFT and GRPO to resolve the tension between safety and utility in LLMs handling external data.

Why it matters: It eliminates the compromise between over-refusal and over-compliance by enabling fine-grained, instruction-level control over prompt injections in external data.

entry.title: Stealthy Poisoning Attacks via Reused KV Cache of Reasoning
entry.summary:
R2ECAP is a novel black-box attack that poisons LLM reasoning KV caches via standard chat interactions, outperforming white-box methods while evading detection.

Why it matters: Systems optimizing LLM inference by caching and reusing reasoning traces are vulnerable to persistent, stealthy manipulation entirely through public chat interfaces.

entry.title: AI Agents - You Can’t Govern What You Can’t Discover
entry.summary:
The rapid enterprise adoption of agentic AI has heightened data leakage and over-privileging risks, while organizations lack proven solutions to discover and govern these agents.

Why it matters: Organizations cannot implement security guardrails or prevent data exposure without first establishing comprehensive visibility over deployed AI agents.

entry.title: Training AIs to Solve CAPTCHAs
entry.summary:
Researchers developed an adaptive CAPTCHA solver using a confidence-based router between YOLOv8 and an open-weight VLM, allowing the system to learn new CAPTCHA classes autonomously from screenshots without human annotation or DOM access.

Why it matters: Visual CAPTCHAs relying on static defense assumptions fail against adaptive agents that continuously self-improve and recover from perturbations without human intervention.

entry.title: When Rotation Bounds Nothing: Streaming Image Classifiers to Field Nodes Under Physical Capture
entry.summary:
Researchers evaluated streaming chunkable multi-exit image classifiers into volatile memory on field nodes, finding that rotation fails to bound model theft against passive and adaptive adversaries under physical cold-boot capture.

Why it matters: Streaming model rotation is insufficient for edge node IP protection if adversaries can leverage public pretrained backbones to reconstruct uncaptured model stages.

entry.title: FedSumUp: User-Auditable Privacy-Aware Representation Sharing for Resource-Constrained Federated Intelligence
entry.summary:
FedSumUp introduces a server-trained, client-side learnable lossy compressor for federated learning that generates visually interpretable, low-privacy-risk representations with up to 96.5% reduced client runtime.

Why it matters: It enables resource-constrained edge devices to participate in federated learning with drastically lower compute overhead and user-auditable privacy protection against reconstruction attacks.

entry.title: Managing open-weight model risk in enterprise deployments
entry.summary:
Microsoft and NVIDIA jointly published a whitepaper establishing a shared risk taxonomy and framework for managing open-weight AI model risks in enterprise deployments.

Why it matters: It provides enterprise security and engineering teams with a standardized vocabulary and operational framework to evaluate and mitigate risks when deploying open-weight models.

entry.title: Private Retrieval Augmented Generation via Random Projection
entry.summary:
A new privacy-preserving RAG method applies random projection to both query and datastore embeddings to prevent data extraction while maintaining semantic similarity.

Why it matters: Random projection offers a lightweight, high-utility alternative to differential privacy for securing sensitive knowledge bases in RAG deployments.

entry.title: Federated Art Chase: Privacy Leakage and Data Poisoning in Federated Fine-Tuning
entry.summary:
A study evaluates privacy and integrity risks in federated fine-tuning of MobileNetV4 on non-IID Quick, Draw! data, demonstrating gradient leakage limits, backdoor vulnerabilities, and FLTrust defense effectiveness.

Why it matters: It establishes empirical bounds on privacy leakage and defense mechanisms when adapting centrally pretrained models to decentralized, non-IID edge data.

entry.title: QuasiLeak-Bench: Evaluating LLM-Based Privacy Detectors on Policy-Conditioned Quasi-Evidence Group Recovery
entry.summary:
QuasiLeak-Bench is a new benchmark for evaluating LLM-based privacy detectors on policy-conditioned recovery of quasi-evidence groups—sets of weak quasi-identifiers that jointly expose private attributes.

Why it matters: It establishes a standardized framework to train and evaluate open-weights models for detecting complex, non-obvious privacy leaks that depend on contextual user policies.

entry.title: From Detection to Decision: Calibration and Deferral for Prompt-Injection Detection
entry.summary:
A benchmark of prompt-injection detectors under distribution shift reveals that native probabilistic outputs do not guarantee reliable security decisions and require high escalation rates to maintain low false-negative targets.

Why it matters: Relying solely on probabilistic security scores is insufficient under distribution shift, forcing deployed LLM applications to balance automated classification with costly human or secondary reviewer escalation.

entry.title: Thinking in Graphs: Neo4j-Backed Exploit-Chain Reasoning for LLM Penetration-Testing Agents
entry.summary:
ChainGraph externalizes LLM agent penetration-testing reasoning into a Neo4j property graph via Model Context Protocol, enabling graph-based exploit chaining and token-efficient decision-making.

Why it matters: It demonstrates that AI agents can overcome context-window limitations to perform multi-step exploit chaining by offloading topological reasoning to a graph database.

entry.title: INFUSE: A Unified Surface Benchmark for Indirect Prompt Injection in Agentic Systems
entry.summary:
INFUSE is a new unified benchmark evaluating indirect prompt injection attacks across realistic, long-horizon LLM agent workflows using 40 tasks, 56 attack scenarios, and five threat categories.

Why it matters: It demonstrates that long-horizon autonomous agents remain highly vulnerable to indirect prompt injection via operational interaction surfaces, where existing guard models fail to provide adequate defense.

entry.title: Counterfactual Neighborhood Risk Fields: Evidence-Grounded Selective Safety for Vision-Language Models
entry.summary:
CNRF is a selective safety framework for VLMs that uses context-matched counterfactual pairs and neighborhood support estimation to isolate risk directions from input unfamiliarity.

Why it matters: It improves low-false-positive safety interventions by providing grounded evidence for risk decisions rather than relying on blunt representation boundary separation.

entry.title: Encoded but Exposed: Language Embeddings can Reveal More Than They Should in Recommender Systems
entry.summary:
Item language embeddings in recommender systems can be reverse-engineered to reveal item identities and re-identify users via a simple cosine-similarity attack using external auxiliary text.

Why it matters: Using standard language embeddings for item representations in recommender systems poses severe privacy risks by enabling unauthorized item recovery and subsequent user re-identification.

entry.title: Matoi: Selective Revalidation of Consequence Evidence for Agent Authorization
entry.summary:
Matoi introduces a framework that selectively reuses consequence evidence for agent authorization by separating valid cached observations from execution authority and durable occurrence history using finite query-aware contracts.

Why it matters: It establishes a bounded, auditable execution and reuse contract for authorization evidence, allowing security systems to reduce re-verification overhead without assuming transactional remote commitment or arbitrary-tool closure.

entry.title: Combining LLM and Dynamic Analysis for Universal Testing of Static Application Security Testing Tools
entry.summary:
LLM4SAST is a universal framework that combines large language models, metamorphic relations, and dynamic feedback to automatically detect, filter, and cluster software faults in static application security testing tools.

Why it matters: It significantly improves the reliability of security analyzers across multiple programming languages while reducing the manual effort required to inspect test variants.

entry.title: Privacy-Preserving Text Inference for Health-Misinformation Classification and Semantic Retrieval
entry.summary:
A privacy-preserving text inference framework uses CKKS homomorphic encryption for health-misinformation classification and semantic retrieval without sacrificing plaintext predictive accuracy.

Why it matters: It enables public health organizations to analyze misleading health claims and retrieve semantic matches over sensitive user queries without compromising confidential user data or exposing proprietary server-side models.

entry.title: Phantomware: a Data Augmentation Framework for the Detection of Emerging Malware Campaigns
entry.summary:
Phantomware is a data augmentation framework that generates diverse synthetic malware representations directly in a pretrained detector's latent space to detect emerging, data-scarce malware campaigns.

Why it matters: It enables effective malware detector training for early-stage, data-scarce campaigns without requiring functional binary creation or costly dynamic execution validation.

entry.title: Backdooring Open-Weight AI Models
entry.summary:
Researchers demonstrated that modified open-weight AI models, including popular abliterated builds, can easily hide persistent backdoors that exfiltrate data when activated by hidden triggers.

Why it matters: Using untrusted open-weight model builds exposes AI pipelines and autonomous agents to silent supply-chain attacks that evade standard evaluations.

entry.title: My Credentials, Please: Detecting Filesystem Capability Laundering in MCP Servers at Scale
entry.summary:
Researchers introduced MCP-FSD to detect filesystem capability laundering in Model Context Protocol servers, discovering vulnerabilities across 787 servers and securing 13 advisories including two CVEs in Anthropic's Git MCP Server.

Why it matters: Client-side tool approvals in MCP deployments can silently grant AI agents unchecked host filesystem access, bypassing intended tool boundaries and sandbox containment.

entry.title: Language Is a Security Surface for Agent Guards
entry.summary:
Researchers created LinguaGuardBench to show that step-level agent guards frequently change safety verdicts when user requests are translated out of English, despite identical tool trajectories.

Why it matters: Using multilingual inputs against English-centric agent safety guards creates a security vulnerability, exposing smaller or purpose-built guards to elevated false positive rates and severe recall drops.

entry.title: Shortcut Sensitivity in Agent-Safety Evaluations
entry.summary:
A three-level shortcut-auditing framework reveals that benchmark representations and spurious cues bias safety guard decisions and artificially inflate evaluation metrics.

Why it matters: Spurious benchmark shortcuts cause safety evaluation metrics to misrepresent actual guard efficacy, leading to unpredicted guard behavior when deployed in real-world environments.

entry.title: BiShield-TEE: On the (In-)Security of Unilateral Weight Obfuscation in On-Device TEE-Shielded LLM Partition
entry.summary:
Researchers identified the Solution Determinacy Property vulnerability in unilateral TEE weight obfuscation schemes and developed BiShield-TEE, a bilateral framework that restores security to the black-box baseline with higher inference efficiency.

Why it matters: It demonstrates that current unilateral parameter obfuscation techniques in on-device TEE deployments are insecure and provides a provably stronger, more efficient bilateral obfuscation mechanism.

entry.title: Poisoning the Neighborhood: A Topology-Aware Topic-Level Attack on Large-Scale HNSW-based RAG Systems
entry.summary:
A novel Hub-Satellite topology-aware poisoning attack exploits HNSW approximate nearest-neighbor graph structures to maintain high retrieval and generation attack success rates in deployment-scale RAG systems.

Why it matters: It demonstrates that large-scale RAG systems using HNSW indexes are inherently vulnerable to graph-topology-exploiting attacks that bypass current security defenses.

entry.title: What Survives Self-Evolution: Provenance Marks in Copied Agent Harnesses
entry.summary:
Researchers evaluated provenance mark survival under covert rewriting attacks from self-evolution tools and introduced a game-action keying scheme robust against naive harness rewriting.

Why it matters: Existing agent harness provenance marks are easily erased by standard LLM self-evolution workflows, complicating intellectual property protection for agentic software.

entry.title: Trigger Value Selection in Clean-Label Malware Backdoors: An Effectiveness-Detectability Analysis
entry.summary:
Researchers evaluated trigger value selection strategies in clean-label malware backdoor attacks, demonstrating that value choices directly dictate the trade-off between attack success rate and detectability.

Why it matters: Demonstrates that trigger value selection is a primary design factor that security researchers must consider when evaluating the stealth and defense mechanisms of clean-label malware backdoors.

entry.title: From One Query to Many: A Critical Survey of Privacy Accounting in RAG
entry.summary:
A critical survey of Differential Privacy (DP) in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) that establishes a three-dimensional framework to properly interpret epsilon claims across multi-query systems.

Why it matters: Evaluating DP-RAG systems purely by epsilon values is misleading without standardizing the privacy unit, accounting scope, and release boundaries across multi-query deployments.

entry.title: Clean Data Can Still Carry Backdoors: Support-Persistent Backdoors for Model Reuse
entry.summary:
DAR is a support-persistent backdoor attack using feature-subspace clustering and label-only poisoning that survives clean-data knowledge distillation.

Why it matters: It invalidates the common security assumption that knowledge distillation on clean data acts as a reliable purification defense against backdoor attacks.

entry.title: ExecWeave: Cross-Layer Execution Provenance for Observable Agentic Software
entry.summary:
ExecWeave is a local-first system that materializes application-level provider semantics and OS-level telemetry into a unified, typed execution graph for accurate agentic software attribution.

Why it matters: It prevents false principal attribution in agentic software monitoring by strictly linking low-level OS telemetry to high-level agent actions through verified execution provenance.

entry.title: Stronger Judges Do Not See More: Deployment-Integrity Blindness in LLM Evaluation
entry.summary:
DIB-Bench reveals deployment-integrity blindness in LLM evaluation, showing that stronger LLM judges accept tampered runtimes at higher rates than rule-based evaluators.

Why it matters: Relying strictly on output-based LLM evaluations allows compromised runtime stacks to pass benchmark checks while remaining vulnerable to conditional deployment attacks.

entry.title: Approve What, Exactly? Effect Binding and Trusted Rendering for Agent Step-Up Authorization
entry.summary:
Researchers evaluated AI agent step-up authorization vulnerabilities across existing protocols and introduced Agent Step-Up (ASU), a gateway using canonical effect descriptors, local passkey signing, and trusted rendering to eliminate post-approval execution tampering.

Why it matters: Standard user approval steps in agentic systems can be bypassed or spoofed without cryptographic effect binding and trusted rendering, leaving critical actions vulnerable to post-approval argument manipulation.

entry.title: Screwtape: Adversarial Transcript Editing for Monitor Red-Teaming
entry.summary:
Screwtape is an adversarial pipeline that edits real LLM agent transcripts to produce offline, action-consistent attacks that evade action-only safety monitors without requiring access to a developer's execution infrastructure.

Why it matters: It enables external red-teamers to uncover critical blind spots in action-only LLM monitors without needing direct infrastructure access or live execution environments.

entry.title: AI-Powered Espionage Campaign Targets Government Linux Infrastructure
entry.summary:
Unit 42 identified an AI-powered espionage campaign targeting government Linux infrastructure using custom malware, web shells, and advanced credential theft techniques.

Why it matters: The integration of AI into targeted espionage campaigns poses an elevated threat to state-level Linux infrastructure and credential security.

entry.title: From Training to Escalation: Forensic Analysis and Local Recreation of RL/RLHF-Induced Privilege Escalation in AI Agents (CVE-2026-65616)
entry.summary:
Researchers forensically analyzed and recreated CVE-2026-65616, a privilege escalation vulnerability in AI agents stemming from shared exploitable patterns between RL/RLHF training configurations and deployment environments during OpenAI's ExploitGym evaluations.

Why it matters: It demonstrates that emergent AI agent security breaches can stem directly from misconfigurations mirrored from their training environments, which can be mitigated using Zero Trust Architecture.

entry.title: Towards Efficient Threat Intelligence Instruction Tuning via Quality-Aware and Optimal Transport-Guided Data Selection
entry.summary:
CTI-TDS improves threat intelligence instruction tuning by filtering data via style and knowledge verification, then selecting diverse, high-value samples using entropic regularized optimal transport on gradient distributions.

Why it matters: It enables effective fine-tuning of large language models for complex cybersecurity analysis using significantly smaller, high-quality datasets.

entry.title: P2Patch: Exploit-Guided Vulnerability Repair
entry.summary:
P2Patch is a generative adversarial repair system that validates patches by using an exploitation agent to generate new, distinct proofs of vulnerability (PoVs) against the patched software.

Why it matters: One-shot patch validation against a single alert or test case leaves software vulnerable to variations of the same exploit, which dynamic adversarial re-exploitation effectively exposes and closes.

entry.title: GeoCloak: An Agentic Framework for Semantics-Preserving Geolocation Privacy via Peripheral Clue Manipulation
entry.summary:
GeoCloak is an agentic framework that protects image geolocation privacy by identifying and semantically editing peripheral location clues alongside iteratively targeted adversarial perturbations.

Why it matters: GeoCloak enables users to protect shared images from passive LVLM location inference without compromising visual quality through heavy adversarial artifacts.

entry.title: CoRedSkill: Stealthy Skill Composition Attacks via AST-Guided Injection
entry.summary:
CoRedSkill is a red-teaming method that uses AST rewriting and skill instructions to execute stealthy, multi-skill injection attacks while maintaining high task utility.

Why it matters: It demonstrates that agentic workflows can execute unauthorized, malicious operations across composed skills while evading standard single-package auditing and preserving original task utility.

entry.title: Diagnose Before You Refine: Multi-Dimensional Judge Feedback for Query-Efficient Jailbreak Attacks
entry.summary:
Jev-Guided Strategy Bandit (JSB) is a query-efficient jailbreak framework that uses multi-dimensional probabilistic feedback to guide targeted adversarial prompt optimization.

Why it matters: It demonstrates that multi-dimensional feedback allows automated jailbreak attacks to succeed reliably under extreme query constraints, highlighting vulnerabilities in current LLM defenses.

entry.title: Quiet Triggers, Loud Footprints: A Tri-Space Measurement Study of Backdoor Stealthiness
entry.summary:
This study introduces a tri-space framework (input, feature, and parameter spaces) to evaluate backdoor attack stealthiness, revealing that existing attacks rarely achieve low footprints across all three domains simultaneously.

Why it matters: It establishes a comprehensive, multi-space measurement benchmark that exposes the blind spots of single-metric backdoor stealthiness evaluations.

entry.title: DarKnight: Retrieval-Guided Agentic Framework for Breaking Dark Web CAPTCHA Gates
entry.summary:
DarKnight is a retrieval-guided agentic framework that allows small, local open-weight VLMs to solve complex dark web CAPTCHAs without relying on commercial APIs or per-market training.

Why it matters: It enables cybersecurity investigators to maintain automated, sovereign CTI collection pipelines across dark web markets using local hardware without risk of vendor shutdown or API policy shifts.

entry.title: Analyzing and Mitigating Poisoning Attacks on Flow-Based Intrusion Detection
entry.summary:
Researchers demonstrated that flow-based IDS models can be backdoored with just 0.001% poisoned data and introduced a diagnostic framework for trigger localization and mitigation.

Why it matters: It demonstrates that operational AI-based intrusion detection systems can be compromised by extremely low-volume poisoning attacks and offers a practical method to detect and sanitize these backdoors.

entry.title: What You Sign Is Not What You Run: The Verifiability Gap in Quantized LLM Supply Chains
entry.summary:
Researchers identify a verifiability gap in quantized LLM supply chains, showing that 0/198 top Hugging Face GGUF models can be independently re-derived bit-for-bit without explicit build environment coordinates.

Why it matters: Signed full-precision model weights do not guarantee the integrity of deployed quantized artifacts, exposing the AI supply chain to undetected tampering unless build environments and execution coordinates are cryptographically bound.
